A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LG-Tok research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching material moved between sections.

before.justification: v1 reports original motion reconstruction and generation results, ablations, motion-editing examples, and runtime measurements on HumanML3D and Motion-X.

after.justification: v2 retains original empirical results and adds KIT-ML evaluation, additional baseline results, and new analyses of token budgets and cross-attention.

M1.justification: The Transformer tokenizer, multi-scale quantization, language conditioning, 10% language-drop probability, motion-space guidance, and masked motion-editing procedure are retained. Expanded explanations and the redrawn framework diagram do not establish an algorithmic change.

E1.justification: v2 adds KIT-ML as a third training and evaluation benchmark, comprising 3,911 motions and 6,278 text annotations, substantially extending dataset coverage. HumanML3D, body-only Motion-X, motion editing, free-form generation, and long-sequence training data were already covered in v1.

E2.justification: DisCoRD is added to both existing benchmark comparisons in Table 2, and ReMoDiffuse appears in the new KIT-ML comparison. The language-drop comparison omits its explicit no-text reference rows when moving from v1 Table 5 to v2 Table 4, although Table 3 retains no-text comparisons.

E3.justification: The added KIT-ML experiments specify guidance scale g=2.0 and include a guidance sweep from 0 to 4. Section 4.1 extends the representation description from meng67 to 64–67-dimensional meng across three datasets. Existing benchmark splits, training budgets, model sizes, and optimization settings remain unchanged.

E4.justification: v2 adds a reconstruction–generation analysis across LG-Tok token budgets (Section 4.7, Table 6), frame-to-word cross-attention case studies (Appendix I, Figure 11), and KIT-ML language-drop ablations and guidance sensitivity results. These substantially expand evidence about compression and alignment. The original regularization analysis largely moves from Appendix C into Section 4.4; it is not wholly new.

E5.justification: Both versions specify 20 evaluations and 95% confidence intervals in Table 2. The new KIT-ML table follows this existing practice. No changed run counts, seed policy, uncertainty-estimation procedure, or significance testing is reported.

E6.justification: v2 adds KIT-ML results, including LG-Tok Top-1/FID of 0.401/0.185 versus MARDM's 0.387/0.242, DisCoRD results, and variant reconstruction measurements. Existing Table 2 LG-Tok scores are unchanged. New Table 6 reports full-model MPJPE of 39.3/31.7, conflicting with the retained Table 3 values of 39.0/31.0; these entries do not establish a same-setting performance improvement.

T1.justification: Equations 1–7 retain the same substantive definitions and reasoning, including autoregressive factorization, quantization, guidance, and temporal editing masks. No new formal assumptions, theorems, proofs, or derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The headline performance claim expands from HumanML3D and Motion-X to three benchmarks including KIT-ML. Preventing shortcut learning becomes explicit in the abstract and contribution list, but its underlying regularization claim already appeared in v1 Appendix C. The central methodological contributions remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds hypotheses about text shortcuts inflating alignment metrics and dataset size affecting token-budget trade-offs, and interprets the new attention maps as word-level alignment. Appendix D supports body-only Motion-X processing with a reported 2.74% frequency of hand/face-related text. Existing memory and training-time limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit code-repository link and states that official scripts perform Motion-X representation conversion. It clarifies the separate LLaMA and CLIP roles and depicts conditional/unconditional decoding passes more explicitly. These are documentation additions; the existing hardware, training-time disclosures, and quantization pseudocode are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to DisCoRD, M2DM, shortcut learning, and KIT-ML, while removing the Nichol–Dhariwal reference. It explicitly distinguishes its learnable queries from M2DM's frame-aligned representation and sharpens the TxtTok comparison. The language-drop novelty argument was already present in v1 Appendix C.

P1.justification: v2 edits the abstract, introduction, related-work discussion, and language-drop explanation; moves the regularization analysis into the main text; and reorders appendix topics. SAR terminology, affiliations, and citation style also change. Most existing methodological and experimental prose remains, making the textual revision more limited than the visual redesign.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to a single-column template with a redesigned title block and headings. Figure 3 is substantially redrawn, the former Figures 6 and 7 are merged, and new trade-off/KIT-ML tables and attention heatmaps are added. Table styling, captions, figure sizing, and placement change throughout.

improvement.justification: KIT-ML evaluation and DisCoRD comparisons broaden validation, while the new trade-off analysis, attention visualizations, and clearer framework diagram make the existing method easier to assess. These provide a limited net gain over v1's already extensive evidence. The unexplained MPJPE disagreement between v2 Tables 6 and 3, together with partly hypothetical mechanism explanations, limits the improvement.
